newsitem.title: USA: Obstacles seen remaining in US, Mexico truck freeze.
newsitem.headline: Obstacles seen remaining in US, Mexico truck freeze.

text.p: Trucking industry officials said Wednesday they hoped the Clinton administration could soon lift a freeze on the crossborder trucking provisions of the North American Free Trade Agreement. But they feared there were still obstacles, mainly on the Mexican side of the issue.

"Yes, I think they (the U.S. administration) want it to happen, but there are still significant obstacles in the way," said Linda Darr, vice president for international affairs at the American Trucking Association. "Mexico is the other negotiating partner. Mexico needs to open its border to us."

Darr said the outstanding issues included the use in Mexico of 53-foot trailers. These are the "trailer of choice" in the United States and Canada, she said, but Mexico published a regulation on January 7 that "is very prohibitive, that would allow 53-foot trailers in a small number of cases."
She said other unresolved issues included small package carrier regulations, the issue of U.S. carrier investment in Mexico, and crossborder access for buses.
Last month, the U.S. trucking, car and freight shipping industries sent President Clinton a letter urging him to end the one-year freeze on NAFTA crossborder trucking provisions.
The freeze was put in place in December 1995 after a coalition of labor and consumer groups argued that Mexico's heavier and older trucks posed safety and environmental hazards to U.S. border states.

The Journal of Commerce reported Wednesday that the Clinton administration had decided to end the freeze. A Department of Transportation spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment on the newspaper report.
